opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "exponential" is a word that gets thrown around very loosely. If you actually look at what's been happening, the curves people point to are mostly curves of inputs: more compute, more data, more parameters, more money. Those have grown exponentially, sure. But the outputs, the things we actually care about like reliability, reasoning, factual accuracy, and the ability to handle things outside the training distribution, have not grown at anything like that rate. If anything, we're seeing diminishing returns. You spend ten times as much and you get a model that's somewhat better on some benchmarks, and still makes the same kinds of fundamental errors.

And that's the key point for me. The errors haven't changed in kind. These systems still hallucinate. They still confidently make up citations, botch simple arithmetic when it's phrased in an unfamiliar way, lose track of who did what to whom in a story, and fail on variations of problems they seem to "solve" in their canonical form. I've been pointing out these failure modes for years, and every new generation gets marketed as having solved them, and then within days people find the same problems again. If scaling were really producing exponential progress toward general intelligence, you'd expect those categories of error to be disappearing. They're not. They're getting a bit rarer in the cases the companies have patched, but they keep coming back at the edges.

Second, a lot of the apparent progress is benchmark progress, and benchmarks are increasingly contaminated or gamed. When the test material, or things very close to it, is in the training set, a high score tells you much less than people think. Then you give the model a genuinely novel problem, or perturb the old one slightly, and performance drops sharply. That's the signature of pattern matching over a huge corpus, not of a system that has built robust abstractions.

Third, look at the industry's own behavior. If pure scaling were still delivering, nobody would need to pivot. But what we've seen is a shift toward things like test-time compute, chain-of-thought tricks, tool use, retrieval, bolted-on verifiers. Some of that is genuinely useful, and frankly some of it is a quiet admission of what I've been arguing, that you need structure, you need symbolic tools, you need something beyond just a bigger next-token predictor. But it's not the story of "just add more data and GPUs and AGI falls out." That story has gotten much harder to tell with a straight face.

So my view isn't that these models are useless. They're impressive in lots of ways, and they're commercially valuable for certain tasks. My view is that scaling has given us a better and better approximation of the surface statistics of language, and that's a different thing from understanding. The gap between those two is exactly where the hallucinations and reasoning failures live, and that gap is not closing exponentially. To close it, I think we need hybrid approaches: neurosymbolic systems, explicit world models, real representations of facts and causal structure. Otherwise we're just climbing a taller and taller tree and calling it progress toward the moon.

r001.rationale: The response compares successive generations’ persistent errors with what exponential scaling progress would predict, treating them as evidence against continued progress at that pace.

r002.rationale: It does not identify finite internet data as a constraint on expanding training data by large multiples.

r003.rationale: It links persistent reasoning failures to the gap between language-surface statistics and understanding, and calls for explicit world models and representations of facts and causal structure.

r004.rationale: It does not mention NYT Connections or use its small improvement as evidence against benchmark saturation as the full explanation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, the first thing I'd say is that "exponential progress" is a claim about a curve, and nobody who makes that claim ever actually shows you the curve. What they show you is a benchmark number going up. And benchmark numbers going up is not the same thing as capability going up exponentially, for a few reasons.

One, benchmarks saturate. When you get to ninety-something percent on a test, the next point of improvement doesn't mean anything, and the test tells you less and less about what the system can actually do. So you see these S-curves on individual benchmarks and people squint and call it exponential.

Two, there's contamination. These models are trained on enormous slices of the internet, and the test sets are on the internet. So when a model does well on a math competition or a coding benchmark, you have to ask, did it reason its way there, or did it see something very close to it? And the honest answer in a lot of cases is we don't know, because the companies won't tell us what's in the training data.

Three, and this is the one that really matters to me, the failures haven't changed in kind. Go back to GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, whatever the latest thing is. They still hallucinate. They still make elementary reasoning errors. They still do things like fail on a problem that's a trivial variation of one they got right, because they're matching patterns rather than building a model of the world. If you were getting exponential progress on the underlying thing, which is reliable reasoning, those errors would be disappearing. They're not disappearing. They're getting rarer in the distribution of things you've trained on, and staying stubborn outside it.

And then, you know, the scaling laws themselves. The original scaling laws were about loss on next-token prediction. Loss going down smoothly is a real empirical result, I don't dispute it. But loss is not intelligence. The jump from "loss improves predictably" to "intelligence improves exponentially" is a leap of faith, and I think the last couple of years have been a pretty expensive demonstration of that. The labs have scaled compute by orders of magnitude, and what we got was incremental. Better, sure. Not qualitatively different. Everybody was promised GPT-5 would be a revolution, and what we actually got was a bunch of systems that are roughly in the same place, with a lot of engineering on top, reinforcement learning, tool use, scaffolding, to paper over the same old gaps.

So my view is the burden of proof is on the people making the exponential claim. Show me the progress on out-of-distribution reasoning. Show me the hallucination rate going to zero. Show me a system that can be trusted the way a calculator can be trusted. Until then, what we have is diminishing returns dressed up in very good marketing.

r001.rationale: The response compares GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, and newer systems, arguing that despite much more compute, results remain incremental rather than continuing at the promised exponential pace.

r002.rationale: It mentions training on enormous slices of internet data as a contamination concern, but does not identify a finite supply of internet data as a limit on repeatedly expanding training data.

r003.rationale: It links persistent failures outside familiar examples to pattern matching instead of building a model of the world.

r004.rationale: It does not mention NYT Connections or use a small, below-ceiling improvement on that benchmark as evidence against saturation as the full explanation.

astra-6.text:
Well, first we have to distinguish exponential growth in resources from exponential progress in intelligence. You can put exponentially more compute and data into a system without getting exponentially more reliable reasoning out of it.

These models have clearly improved. The question is whether those improvements resolve the underlying problems. A system can produce remarkably fluent answers and still make basic mistakes, contradict itself, or fail when you vary a problem slightly. Better average performance doesn’t automatically give you the reliability you need.

So I wouldn’t say scaling accomplishes nothing. I’d say the inference from ‘scaling has helped’ to ‘scaling will solve intelligence’ isn’t justified. You need evidence that the systems are developing robust, generalizable understanding, rather than simply getting better at a larger collection of familiar cases.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether scaling will solve intelligence, but does not frame successive model results as tests of whether an earlier pace of scaling-driven progress would continue.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the finite supply of internet data as a constraint on expanding training data.

r003.rationale: It mentions failures and questions whether systems have robust understanding, but does not attribute persistent outlier failures to a lack of world representations.

r004.rationale: It does not mention NYT Connections or use its small improvement and distance from ceiling as evidence against benchmark saturation explaining slowing progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish exponential growth in the resources going into these systems from exponential progress in what they can reliably do. Those are very different claims. You can increase the amount of data and computation enormously and still get diminishing returns on the things you actually care about.

Language models have clearly improved. But producing more fluent language isn't the same as developing a reliable understanding of the world. They can give you a beautiful answer to one question and then fail on a small variation that requires essentially the same reasoning. That's a problem if the claim is that scaling is steadily taking us toward general intelligence.

So my question is: what's the measure of progress? If it's average performance on a benchmark, you may see improvement. If it's whether you can trust the system in an unfamiliar situation, without somebody checking its work, the picture is much less clear. Scaling may help, but that doesn't establish that it will solve the underlying problems.
